one_liner: Zig DOM/streaming XML parser whose default permissive mode beats pugixml and rapidxml by 1.5-5.4x on real-world files.
what_it_does: A dependency-free Zig library that parses an in-memory UTF-8 XML buffer into a compact, index-based, read-only DOM (12-byte nodes with the default u32 indexes), or emits events to a callback through a streaming parser that also accepts growing buffers incrementally with save/restore. The API is not pugixml-shaped: a comptime ParseOptions value (destructive or non_destructive, validate_well_formedness, stored last-child/prev-sibling links, misc nodes, DTD entity expansion) generates the concrete Document, Node and StreamingParser types. Nodes expose name/value slices, raw or decoded attribute lookup, child/sibling/parent navigation, a small tag/#id/.class/[attr] selector matcher, and write() serialization. There is no DOM mutation API and no XPath.
how_it_is_fast: It builds a lazy, source-backed DOM. Each node stores only a parent index and one source span, and text nodes are marked by a reversed span instead of a kind field. Attributes are not tokenized during parsing; they are rescanned from the source when queried. Subtree and sibling bounds come from preorder parent links, so parsing writes little more than 12 bytes per node. In the default permissive mode, a start tag ends at the first '>' found by a SIMD scan (portable Zig @Vector: 32 bytes with AVX2, 16 bytes elsewhere), with quote parity checked in bulk instead of running a per-attribute state machine. Text runs are also found with vector compare masks, and the common <tag>text</tag> shape is special-cased with a u64 comparison of the first 8 name bytes. Node storage is pre-sized from a '<'-density sample, small documents start in a 64-node on-stack buffer, and inputs of 64 KiB or more that repeat one exact token take dedicated repeated-document paths, which produce the 8.9-9.7x synthetic results. Well-formedness validation (UTF-8 and XML character checks, duplicate-attribute filter, tag matching, reference checks) is a separate code path chosen at compile time, which is why it roughly halves throughput.
when_to_use: Zig programs that parse many small-to-medium UTF-8 documents (RSS/Atom feeds, sitemaps, catalogs, config) into a read-only tree: 2.1-4.1x pugixml on the 0.2-23 KiB feed and catalog fixtures (derived from page data).
Trusted or producer-controlled XML where lenient parsing is acceptable and you can give the parser a mutable buffer that outlives the Document.
Read patterns that touch only a few attributes or text values: attribute scanning and entity decoding wait until you query them, so content you never read costs almost nothing.

Chunked or event-driven ingestion in Zig: the streaming parser takes cumulative buffers with save/restore, and it runs at 0.79-1.23x the DOM's throughput on the real-world fixtures (derived from page data).
when_not_to_use: C or C++ codebases: there is no C ABI or binding (build.zig exposes only a Zig module), so replacing pugixml means writing and maintaining a wrapper.

Untrusted input that must be well-formed: validate_well_formedness drops the mean to 2037.12 MiB/s. It then loses to pugixml on weekly_utf8.xml (0.57x) and synthetic_deep_tree.xml (0.89x), and to rapidxml on 5 of the 14 real or pugixml-corpus files that have a validated result (derived from page data).

Workloads that need DOM editing, XPath or non-UTF-8 input. zxml has no mutation API and no XPath. The source handles only UTF-8 (plus a UTF-8 BOM), with no transcoding found, while pugixml converts UTF-16/32 and Latin-1.

Very large documents: the largest real-world fixture is a ~2.1 MiB arXiv feed (3.2x pugixml), most real files are 0.2-23 KiB (sizes derived from latest.json), and default u32 indexes reject inputs over 4 GiB - 1 with InputTooLarge unless you build with -Dintlen=u64.

Production code that needs a track record: v0.1.0 in build.zig.zon, no tags or releases, one contributor, 0 stars, no issues or PRs ever filed, and it requires exactly the Zig 0.16 toolchain generation.

integration.dependencies: none (Zig standard library only; the benchmarks use pugixml and rapidxml, fetched separately)
integration.platforms: any Zig target. SIMD uses portable @Vector (32-byte with AVX2 on x86, 16-byte elsewhere). ReleaseSafe compile checks passed for x86_64/aarch64 Linux, Windows and macOS, RISC-V 64, PowerPC64, ARM and x86_64 FreeBSD. Benchmarks exist only for x86_64 (i5-12450H).
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. In the default destructive mode the decoding accessors (getAttributeValue, value, innerText) rewrite the input buffer and node spans in place, so a Document shared across threads needs external locking. In non_destructive mode those accessors appear to be read-only (inferred from src/document.zig).

gotchas: The default ParseOptions{} is destructive: parse takes a []u8, and decoded accessors compact entity-containing values in place, so the original bytes are gone. Set non_destructive = true to parse a []const u8.

Permissive mode recovers silently. `` and an unclosed `` both parse without error, and unquoted attributes such as a=1 are accepted. A raw '>' inside a quoted attribute value, however, may be rejected; use > or enable validation.

By default, whitespace-only text nodes are dropped, comments and PIs are not stored (include_misc_nodes = false), and DTD entities are not expanded (expand_dtd_entities = false, capped by max_entity_value_len when on). Decoded-value results may own memory and must be released with .free(allocator).

Without store_prev_sibling or store_last_child, prevSibling and lastChild scan forward from the parent, and nextSibling walks the current node's whole subtree. Backward or last-child navigation over wide or deep trees can be much slower than pugixml's linked nodes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick zxml when you are working in Zig and want both a lazy DOM and an incremental streaming parser without C interop. In C++, the catalogued LightningXML (3.82 GB/s vs pugixml 1.46 GB/s on its flat workload) and Parshred (1.6-3.3x pugixml) link directly. simdxml suits XPath-style queries over multi-GB files, which zxml neither supports nor has measured.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's stable-profile run on an i5-12450H (Linux 7.2, x86_64), zxml's default permissive DOM (Zig 0.16.0, ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native) beat the faster of pugixml (pinned git revision) and rapidxml 1.13 on all 24 headline fixtures. The C++ parsers were built with an unidentified system c++ driver at -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native. The margin was 1.47-5.41x on the 15 real-world and pugixml-corpus files and reached 9.73x on synthetic exact-repeat inputs, and the mean was 3799.40 MiB/s vs 1312.83 for pugixml. The harness has three imbalances: pugixml's load_buffer copies the input on every iteration, pugixml builds comment/PI/declaration/doctype nodes while zxml's default stores none, and the validated DOM averages only 2037.12 MiB/s (about 1.55x pugixml).
status_note: Actively developed by a single author (about 290 commits since April 2026, last commit 2026-09-09) but still unreleased at v0.1.0; it is MIT-licensed, pure Zig and easy to vendor as a module if you pin Zig 0.16.0.
